articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fund, the county has completed exactly two drainage projects. Where did the money go?
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.3 million from the stormwater utility fee since 2023 but completed only two drainage projects
County documents show $31 million sits in reserve accounts while 847 drainage complaints remain unresolved
Officials blame permitting delays and staff shortages, but records reveal the county has hired zero new stormwater engineers since the fee's approval
articles.body:
The water stands three feet deep in Martha Gonzalez's front yard every time it rains more than an inch. She knows because she measured it. She's been measuring since 2019.

"I voted for that stormwater fee," Gonzalez said, standing on her porch on Doolittle Road in Warrington. "They said it would fix the drainage. That was three years ago."

Her neighborhood appears on the county's stormwater priority list. Number 47 out of 312 projects. The county has completed two.

The Money Trail

Escambia County voters approved the stormwater utility fee in November 2022 by a margin of 58 to 42 percent. The fee—$7.50 per month for most residential properties—was projected to generate $15 million annually for drainage improvements.

It has performed better than expected. County financial records obtained through a public records request show the fee brought in $14.8 million in fiscal year 2023, $15.9 million in 2024, and $16.6 million in 2025. Total collections through May 2026: $47.3 million.

Total spent on completed construction projects: $4.1 million.

The remaining $43.2 million breaks down like this, according to county documents: $31 million in reserve accounts, $8.7 million allocated to projects in "design phase," and $3.5 million spent on administrative costs including staff salaries, equipment, and consulting fees.

The two completed projects—a culvert replacement on Lillian Highway and a retention pond expansion near Beulah—addressed 23 properties total.

847 Complaints and Counting

The county's stormwater complaint database, also obtained through public records, lists 847 unresolved drainage complaints as of June 1, 2026. Some date back to 2017. The database shows 1,247 total complaints filed since the stormwater fee took effect. The county has closed 400, though "closed" includes complaints marked "no action warranted" or "referred to other agency."

District 2 Commissioner Janet Bradley raised concerns about the backlog at a May board meeting.

"We told voters this money would fix their flooding," Bradley said. "Three years later, I'm getting the same calls from the same people about the same flooded streets."

Public Works Director Thomas Hadley defended the pace at that meeting, citing permitting requirements, environmental reviews, and supply chain delays for drainage pipe.

"These are complex infrastructure projects," Hadley said. "We can't just dig a ditch. There are federal and state regulations we have to follow."

The Staffing Question

The original stormwater fee proposal, presented to commissioners in September 2022, included plans to hire eight new positions: four stormwater engineers, two project managers, and two field inspectors. The positions were budgeted at $890,000 annually.

County HR records show the stormwater division currently employs the same number of staff it did before the fee passed. Zero new engineers. Zero new project managers. One field inspector hired in 2024 to replace a retirement.

When asked about the staffing discrepancy, county spokesman Derek Moore said positions have been "difficult to fill" due to competition from private engineering firms.

"We've posted these positions multiple times," Moore said in an email. "The applicant pool has been limited."

Job posting records tell a different story. The county posted one stormwater engineer position in March 2024. It offered a salary range of $52,000 to $61,000. The Florida Engineering Society's 2024 salary survey lists the median starting salary for civil engineers in the Pensacola market at $68,500.

The posting closed after 30 days with four applicants. None were hired. The position has not been reposted.

Reserve Fund Questions

The $31 million sitting in reserve accounts has drawn scrutiny from commissioners in both parties. District 4 Commissioner Robert Cole, who voted against the original fee, called the reserves "a slush fund" at the May meeting.

County Administrator Wes Moreno pushed back on that characterization.

"These reserves are committed to specific projects," Moreno said. "We can't spend money on construction until design is complete and permits are in hand. This is responsible financial management."

But the county's own project timeline documents suggest otherwise. Of the 23 projects listed as "in design," 14 have been in that phase for more than 18 months. Six have no design contract assigned. Three show no activity in county project management software since 2024.

The Doolittle Road project—Martha Gonzalez's neighborhood—entered the design phase in April 2024. It has not progressed since. No design firm has been contracted. No permits have been applied for. The project file contains a single document: a 2023 drainage study that identified the area as "critical need."

What Happens Next

Commissioner Bradley has requested a full audit of the stormwater fund, to be conducted by the county's internal auditor. That audit is scheduled to begin in August, with results expected by November.

Meanwhile, hurricane season is here. The National Weather Service's seasonal outlook calls for above-average tropical activity in the Gulf. Escambia County's emergency management website advises residents in flood-prone areas to "take precautions" and "know their evacuation routes."

Gonzalez has heard that advice before. She keeps sandbags stacked by her garage now. She bought them herself.

"Every time there's a storm coming, they tell us to prepare," she said. "I've been preparing for seven years. When are they going to prepare?"

The Flightline will continue reporting on the stormwater fund audit and any developments in county drainage projects.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Fishermen of Joe Patti's Waterfront
articles.dek: As condo towers rise along the bayou, a shrinking fleet of commercial boats still unloads at dawn. The families who work them aren't sure how many seasons they have left.
brief: Only 12 commercial fishing boats still operate from Joe Patti's waterfront, down from more than 40 two decades ago
Rising property values and development pressure threaten the last working waterfront in Pensacola
Third-generation fishing families face an uncertain future as costs climb and the next generation looks elsewhere
articles.body:
The diesel engines cough to life at 4:47 a.m. A pelican lifts off the piling closest to the fuel dock, annoyed. Tommy Nguyen stands on the stern of the Miss Saigon II, coiling rope in the dark while his father checks the ice hold one more time.

Behind them, across Bayou Chico, a construction crane holds still against the purple sky. The skeleton of a seven-story condominium complex rises where Sampson's Boat Repair stood for 60 years. By the time the Nguyens return this afternoon with their catch, workers will be pouring concrete on the fourth floor.

"Every year there's something new over there," Tommy says, nodding toward the crane. "Every year there's one less of us over here."

He's 34 years old. He's been fishing these waters since he was eight. He isn't sure his own kids will have the chance.

A Shrinking Fleet

The commercial fishing fleet at Joe Patti's Seafood numbered more than 40 boats in 2005. This morning, 12 remain. The names painted on their transoms read like a census of Pensacola's working waterfront: Miss Saigon II, Lady Patricia, Sweet Caroline, Reel Lucky. Vietnamese families. Croatian families. Families whose people have fished the Gulf since before Florida was a state.

They unload at the same concrete dock where Joe Patti himself bought snapper and grouper in the 1930s. The retail market that bears his name still opens at 7 a.m., still sells fresh catch to tourists and locals who line up along Devilliers Street. But less and less of that fish comes off local boats.

"Maybe 30 percent of what we sell now is caught by these guys," says Marcus Webb, who manages purchasing for Joe Patti's Seafood. "Used to be 70, 80 percent. The demand is there. The boats aren't."

Webb pulls a clipboard from under the counter. This week's local haul: 2,100 pounds of red snapper, 800 pounds of vermilion, 340 pounds of triggerfish. The rest comes from distributors in Louisiana, Texas, the Carolinas. Some comes from overseas.

"People come here thinking everything in the case came off that dock," Webb says. "I wish it did."

The Economics of Staying Afloat

Captain Mike Radich has worked commercial boats in Pensacola for 41 years. He owns the Lady Patricia, a 52-foot snapper boat he bought in 1998 for $85,000. Today, the same vessel would cost $400,000 or more. His fuel bill last month came to $6,200. Insurance runs $14,000 a year. Dock fees at Joe Patti's: $800 monthly, up from $400 five years ago.

"The math doesn't math anymore," Radich says. He's sitting on an overturned five-gallon bucket, mending a tear in his net. His hands are scarred and sun-spotted. "My daddy did this. His daddy did this. But I'm not pushing my boys into it."

His sons are 28 and 25. One works construction. The other manages a restaurant in Gulf Breeze.

The federal quota system doesn't help. Red snapper season for commercial fishermen runs just a few months. Allocation fights between recreational and commercial sectors have grown bitter. Radich says his individual fishing quota—the pounds he's legally allowed to catch—hasn't increased in a decade, even as operating costs doubled.

"They keep squeezing us from both ends," he says. "Government on one side, money on the other."

Development Closes In

The waterfront around Joe Patti's has transformed in the past decade. What was once a working-class neighborhood of boat repair shops, net houses, and cinder-block fish markets now features boutique hotels, waterfront townhomes, and the promise of more.

In 2024, Escambia County approved a zoning variance for the Bayou Chico Marina District, a mixed-use development on 12 acres just east of Joe Patti's. The project includes 280 residential units, 40,000 square feet of retail space, and a 120-slip marina marketed primarily to recreational boaters.

The developers, Atlanta-based Tidemark Communities, emphasized "maritime heritage" in their presentations to county commissioners. Renderings showed kayakers, paddleboarders, and families dining at waterfront cafes. No commercial fishing boats appeared in the images.

"We're not against fishing," Tidemark spokesperson Dana Whitfield said in an email. "We're creating a destination that celebrates Pensacola's coastal character."

But commercial captains see the future clearly. More recreational boats means more competition for dock space, more complaints about diesel fumes and early-morning noise, more pressure to relocate.

"They want the aesthetic," says Linh Nguyen, Tommy's father and owner of the Miss Saigon II. "They don't want the smell."

He came to Pensacola in 1982, part of the wave of Vietnamese refugees who rebuilt the Gulf Coast fishing industry. He learned the waters from Croatians and Greeks who'd worked them for generations. He raised three children on snapper and shrimp money. Now he wonders if there's a place for people like him in the Pensacola being built around him.

"This is my home," he says. "But home is changing."

What Protection Exists

Florida law offers some safeguards for working waterfronts. The Florida Working Waterfront Act, passed in 2005, created property tax relief for commercial fishing operations and established the Waterfronts Florida Partnership to help communities preserve maritime industry.

Pensacola has participated in the program since 2008. But local advocates say the protections haven't kept pace with development pressure.

"The tax break helps, but it doesn't address the fundamental problem," says Rachel Dominguez, director of the Gulf Coast Maritime Heritage Foundation. "When surrounding property values explode, the pressure to sell becomes overwhelming. One bad season, one health crisis, and these families are looking at a buyout offer that could set them up for life."

Dominguez's organization has lobbied Escambia County to establish a commercial fishing preservation zone around Joe Patti's—dedicated dock space that couldn't be converted to recreational use without a supermajority vote of county commissioners. The proposal has stalled in committee twice.

"There's sympathy for the idea," she says. "There's not political will."

County Commissioner Ray Bergosh, whose district includes the waterfront, says he supports commercial fishing but questions whether government intervention is the answer.

"These are market forces," Bergosh said at a February commission meeting. "I'm not sure it's our role to pick winners and losers."

The Morning's Catch

By 3 p.m., the Miss Saigon II is back at the dock. The Nguyens have been on the water for ten hours. They're unloading 380 pounds of red snapper, 220 pounds of vermilion, a few dozen pounds of amberjack. It's a decent haul. Not great.

Tommy's hands move automatically, tossing fish into the sorting bins his father holds steady. They don't talk. They don't need to. This is a rhythm learned over decades, passed from generation to generation through repetition, not instruction.

Across the bayou, the construction crane swings a load of rebar toward the fourth floor. A backup alarm beeps. A seagull screams.

Inside Joe Patti's, the afternoon crowd browses the display cases. Tourists take photos of the mounted fish on the walls. A young couple asks the counter worker which snapper is freshest.

"That one," he says, pointing to a red snapper fillet glistening on ice. "Came in about an hour ago. Local boat."

They buy two pounds. They don't ask which boat. They don't know the name Nguyen. They don't know that the man who caught their dinner has been doing this for 44 years, or that his son isn't sure he'll make it to 44 himself.

Outside, Tommy hoses down the deck of the Miss Saigon II. His father has already gone to settle up with the fish house. The sun is dropping toward the bayou, painting the construction crane gold.

"Same time tomorrow," Tommy says to no one in particular.

The pelican settles back onto its piling. The diesel engine ticks as it cools. Somewhere in the distance, a backup alarm beeps again.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's New Flight Pattern Brings More Noise to East Hill
articles.dek: Residents say the Navy changed training routes without warning. The base says nothing changed. Flight-tracking data tells a different story.
brief: East Hill residents report significant increase in low-altitude military aircraft noise since April
NAS Pensacola Public Affairs states no official changes to training flight patterns have occurred
ADS-B flight tracking data shows T-6 Texan II trainers now routing directly over residential neighborhoods that previously saw minimal traffic
articles.body:
The orange trees in Martha Keegan's backyard were planted by her grandfather in 1952. She's picked satsumas from them every December for 61 years. This spring, she started picking up the fruit early—shaken loose by the roar of Navy trainers passing 800 feet above her roof.

"It used to be maybe once a day you'd hear something," Keegan said, standing in her yard on 12th Avenue. "Now it's every fifteen minutes. Sometimes closer together. My dog won't go outside anymore."

Keegan is one of dozens of East Hill residents who have contacted city council members, the mayor's office and NAS Pensacola since April complaining about a dramatic increase in military aircraft noise over their neighborhood. The complaints describe low-flying planes, sometimes in rapid succession, disrupting sleep and startling pets and children.

The Navy says nothing has changed.

"Training Wing Six has not implemented any modifications to established flight patterns or training routes," NAS Pensacola Public Affairs Officer Lt. Commander David Reyes wrote in an email response to questions from The Flightline. "Flight operations continue in accordance with long-standing procedures."

But flight-tracking data reviewed by The Flightline tells a different story.

What the data shows

ADS-B Exchange, a publicly accessible flight-tracking service that aggregates transponder data from aircraft, reveals a clear pattern shift beginning in mid-April. T-6B Texan II turboprops—the primary trainer aircraft for Navy and Marine Corps student aviators at NAS Pensacola—now routinely fly a departure path that crosses directly over East Hill between 12th and 17th Avenues.

Prior to April 14, the same aircraft typically turned south immediately after takeoff from Runway 26, routing over Bayou Texar and largely avoiding the dense residential grid north of Cervantes Street. The Flightline reviewed tracking data from January through June and found the route change occurred abruptly and has remained consistent for two months.

On a single day last week—June 9—ADS-B data showed 34 T-6B flights crossing over the 1400 block of East Blount Street between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. The same location showed four such flights on a comparable day in February.

When presented with this data, Lt. Commander Reyes did not dispute the findings but declined to comment further. "I'd refer you to our previous statement," he wrote.

'We're not anti-military'

East Hill has coexisted with NAS Pensacola for over a century. The base predates most of the neighborhood's housing stock. Residents who spoke to The Flightline were careful to note their complaints aren't about the base's existence or mission.

"My father was a naval aviator. I grew up on this base," said Tom Whitfield, who lives on East Strong Street. "We're not anti-military. We just want to know why this changed and whether anybody thought about the people underneath before they drew new lines on a map."

Whitfield started a group text with neighbors in late April after multiple people mentioned the noise independently. The group now has 43 members. Several have filed formal complaints with the base, the city and the Federal Aviation Administration.

FAA spokesperson Maria Santos confirmed the agency has received 12 noise complaints related to NAS Pensacola since April 1, compared to two during the same period last year. However, Santos noted the FAA has limited authority over military flight operations.

"Military airspace and procedures are generally exempt from FAA noise abatement requirements," Santos said. "Complaints are forwarded to the relevant military installation."

What could explain the change

Military aviation experts contacted by The Flightline offered several possible explanations for an unofficial route change.

"Sometimes it's as simple as a new instructor who prefers a different departure," said Rick Jameson, a retired Navy pilot who flew trainers at Pensacola in the 1990s. "If the new way isn't explicitly prohibited, it can become habit. Then it spreads."

Another possibility: construction or maintenance on the base that temporarily closed a taxiway or changed preferred runway usage. NAS Pensacola's official website lists ongoing infrastructure projects but does not specify impacts to flight operations.

A third explanation is increased training tempo. The Navy has publicly discussed accelerating pilot production to address shortfalls. More flights could mean more route variations.

None of these explanations require an official policy change—which may be why the Navy can accurately state that no such change occurred while residents experience something dramatically different.

What happens next

Pensacola City Council Member Allison Patton, whose District 6 includes much of East Hill, said she's requested a meeting with base leadership.

"We've had a good working relationship with NAS Pensacola on noise issues in the past," Patton said. "When Whiting Field was doing more night flights a few years ago, we were able to have a conversation. I'm hoping for the same here."

Patton said she expects to meet with base representatives sometime in the next two weeks. She's asked constituents to continue documenting noise incidents with dates and times.

For Martha Keegan, the timing matters. Her grandson turns two in August. Last year's birthday party was in the backyard, under the satsuma trees.

"I don't know if we can do that this year," she said. "You can't have a conversation out here anymore. You can't hear yourself think."

She looked up at the empty sky, quiet for the moment.

"I keep waiting for someone to just tell us the truth about what changed. That's all we want. Just tell us what happened."
